document.title: Report on Afghanistan to the Central Committee CPSU, by A. Gromyko, Y. Andropov, D. Ustinov, B. Ponomarev
document.authors: A. Gromyko, Y. Andropov, D. Ustinov, B. Ponomarev (published in Lyakhovsky)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979: Not Trump’s Terrorists, Nor Zbig’s Warm Water Ports | National Security Archive
document.note: Crucial end-of-October 1979 report to the Central Committee from the Politburo subcommittee assessing Afghanistan. It points to the importance of Amin's meeting with the Americans and the suspicions it raised in Moscow, including the need to prevent counter-revolution or Amin's political re-orientation towards the West.

key_claims: Soviet leaders judged the situation in Afghanistan extremely complicated after Amin's September 1979 removal and killing of Taraki.
Repression within the Party, army, state apparatus and civic organizations widened under Amin despite superficial liberalizing gestures.
Amin was reported to be planning executions of Politburo members Zerai, Misak and Pandzhshiri.
Amin promoted loyalists and relatives into PDPA ruling organs.
Soviet leaders saw signs Amin might pursue a more balanced policy toward Western powers, and US contacts suggested possible reorientation toward Washington.
Recommended policy was to keep working with Amin, avoid signaling distrust, and propose further measures only if he turned anti-Soviet.
